doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: Between Curtis and the black music world
summary: Gold explains blues bands, Huff and Bell, a poor North Philly upbringing, playing the Latin Casino against Curtis's wishes, and giving up cello and bass for arranging.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I don't want to make too much out of this but it seems to me when you were making this decision at 17 according to your promo here, that you had one foot in the white world of music and you had another in the black world of music. Were you aware of that? Was that partly your decision to go — to leave Curtis and go in this other direction?

Well you know at that moment it was the hippie days so I was playing in a few bands. The bands were based on blues. Blues obviously the derivative of blues is black music, the church the old work songs, every — all that. You know? So yeah I was fascinated. I was also fascinated by popular music in general. But in Philadelphia the people that were really adept that I met were people like Leon Huff and people like, you know they were Tommy Bell and they were really crazily talented people that weren't talented like the fiddle players at Curtis, like the violinists at Curtis, but in a whole different way off the top of their head and involving the black church and a lot of things. It was fascinating. Plus I grew up in a very poor neighborhood. My father had a hardware toy store in North Philly, which was a very mixed neighborhood to begin with. So yes I knew that I had, in those days I don't think today — if you're a classical musician, you go to Juilliard, you can come out and frame your classical background or your jazz background in a whole lot of different light than you used to be able to in the '60s. It's a different world today than it was then. You either had to go one route, the long hair route, which was classical music or you had to go the other route which was almost giving that up. Curtis hated that I used to play at the Latin Casino to make a buck. You know? I mean in those days if I made a few hundred dollars a week that was amazing. I could live forever on it.
In the string sections. Okay. But you became a bass player.

I did play bass too, and I played guitar too. But I gave them up when, in the '70s, when the '70s really started rolling and I started arranging and making records and doing all that stuff I didn't play the bass anymore. I barely played the cello anymore.
